### Federal-prisoner limitation and successive-motion certification

**Governing question:** The new §2255 limitation period and certification for a second or successive motion.

**Current rule:** A §2255 motion has a one-year limitation running from the latest of conviction finality; removal of an unlawful governmental filing impediment that actually prevented the motion; initial Supreme Court recognition of the asserted newly recognized right made retroactively applicable on collateral review; or when due diligence could discover the supporting facts. A second or successive motion requires certification under §2244 by an appropriate appellate panel of either newly discovered evidence which, if proved and considered with all evidence, would establish clearly and convincingly that no reasonable factfinder would have found guilt, or a previously unavailable new constitutional rule made retroactive on collateral review by the Supreme Court. The evidence route has its own text and is not silently replaced with §2244(b)(2)(B)’s distinct state-prisoner constitutional-error/diligence formulation.

**Authority by component:**

- Latest-event period and alternative certification predicates: Source, authority and operative text, Public Law 104-132, Title I, §105(2), amended 28 U.S.C. §2255 limitation and successive-motion paragraphs, enacted 1996-04-24; the Record’s retained complete enacted text supplies these components.

**Present operation effective:** AEDPA enactment, 1996-04-24.

**Effective transition:** Enacted April 24, 1996. Unlike chapter 154’s express pending-case clause, temporal application of the other Title I amendments to a particular pending proceeding is unresolved except for the specified post-enactment authorization/review channel adjudicated in Felker. Neither universal retroactivity nor universal prospective-only treatment is established.

**Exceptions and limits:** The amendment supplies no conclusion that an earlier dismissal makes a later motion successive, that a particular deadline has expired, or that collateral relief is guaranteed.

### Second or successive state-custody habeas applications

**Governing question:** Repeated/new claims, appellate authorization and district verification under amended §2244(b).

**Current rule:** A claim in a second or successive §2254 application already presented in a prior application must be dismissed. A new claim must also be dismissed unless it relies on a previously unavailable new constitutional rule made retroactive on collateral review by the Supreme Court, or both its factual predicate was not previously discoverable through due diligence and its facts, if proved and viewed with all evidence, would establish clearly and convincingly that but for constitutional error no reasonable factfinder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense. Before district filing, the applicant must seek appropriate appellate authorization; a three-judge panel may authorize only on a prima facie showing of these requirements and must act within thirty days. A grant or denial is not appealable and cannot be the subject of rehearing or certiorari. Authorization is not final entitlement: the district court must dismiss unless the applicant establishes the statutory conditions.

**Authority by component:**

- Separate repeated/new claim restrictions and two-stage authorization/verification: Source, authority and operative text, Public Law 104-132, Title I, §106(b), 28 U.S.C. §2244(b)(1)–(4), enacted 1996-04-24; the Record’s retained complete enacted text supplies these components.
- Post-enactment authorization-review bar and distinction from original filing: The withdrawn review route and retained original jurisdiction; Temporal operation of the channel rule; Successive restrictions and original-writ discretion, 1996-06-28. Felker Part I-A and II, all nine; the channel temporal result has all nine, its Part I-B explanation Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer (six).

**Present operation effective:** Statutory requirements enacted 1996-04-24; Felker’s specified review-channel construction, 1996-06-28.

**Effective transition:** Enacted April 24, 1996. Unlike chapter 154’s express pending-case clause, temporal application of the other Title I amendments to a particular pending proceeding is unresolved except for the specified post-enactment authorization/review channel adjudicated in Felker. Neither universal retroactivity nor universal prospective-only treatment is established.

**Exceptions and limits:** A request to announce a new rule is not reliance on an existing Supreme Court rule made retroactive. Schlup’s gateway and §2244(b)(2)(B)’s cumulative conditions are not interchangeable. The district authorization mechanism does not govern Supreme Court original filing; direct mandatory force of paragraphs (1)–(2) there remains reserved.

**Holdings navigation:** Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651 (1996).

### Supreme Court original habeas after an authorization-review bar

**Governing question:** The retained original-writ channel and extraordinary showing following §2244(b)(3)(E).

**Current rule:** The statutory ban on ordinary certiorari review of a circuit’s successive-application authorization decision does not repeal §2241’s distinct Supreme Court original habeas authority. An original petition receives independent consideration rather than appellate review of that authorization judgment. Circuit permission to file in district court is not a prerequisite to filing here. Sections 2244(b)(1)–(2) inform original-writ discretion; whether they bind it directly remains unresolved. Rule 20 separately requires an explanation for not seeking district relief, how and where state remedies were exhausted or §2254(b) otherwise satisfied, exceptional circumstances warranting the Supreme Court’s discretionary exercise and lack of adequate relief in another form or court. Retained jurisdiction alone does not warrant the writ, further proceedings or an execution stay. Section 1651 aids independently held jurisdiction rather than supplying a freestanding new source.

**Authority by component:**

- Separate jurisdiction and original-writ discretion: The withdrawn review route and retained original jurisdiction; Successive restrictions and original-writ discretion; The separate constitutional innocence claim and original relief, 1996-06-28; Felker Parts I-A, II and IV-B, all nine.

**Present operation effective:** Felker, 1996-06-28.

**Exceptions and limits:** Felker’s as-applied constitutional rejection rests on actual independent consideration and an adequate traditional original-writ ground, not approval of eliminating every meaningful forum. Constitutional innocence’s universal merits threshold, other supervisory routes, and the constitutionality of all AEDPA restrictions remain open.

**Holdings navigation:** Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651 (1996).

### Qualifying State counsel systems for special capital habeas procedures

**Governing question:** Conditions for chapter 154 and its separate unitary-review route.

**Current rule:** Chapter 154 applies to state-custody §2254 capital cases only when the State satisfies its counsel-system conditions. Under §2261(b)–(c), a statute, highest-court rule or other state-authorized agency mechanism must provide competent appointed counsel, compensation and reasonable litigation expenses for indigent capital postconviction review after the conviction and sentence are upheld on direct appeal to the State’s court of last resort or otherwise become final for State-law purposes, with appointment-competency standards supplied by statute or court rule. The mechanism must offer counsel to all prisoners under capital sentence and require a court-of-record order appointing counsel for an indigent prisoner who accepts or cannot competently choose, finding an informed rejection after a hearing if necessary, or denying appointment on a nonindigency finding. Trial or direct-appeal counsel cannot serve unless both prisoner and counsel expressly request continuity. Under §2261(e), state/federal collateral counsel ineffectiveness or incompetence is no §2254 relief ground but does not bar replacing counsel on the court’s own or prisoner’s motion at any postconviction stage. Section 2265 separately qualifies a unitary-review system permitting collateral claims during direct review: a statute or highest-court rule must provide competent counsel, compensation and reasonable expenses including collateral-claim litigation, and the statute or highest-court rule must prescribe appointment-competency standards; an offer and §2261(c)-type order follow trial, and trial counsel cannot continue absent both parties’ express request. For a qualifying unitary procedure, §§2262–2264 and 2266 apply with direct/postconviction references read as unitary review. If the transcript is unavailable at the posttrial representation order, the 180-day filing period starts only when a transcript is supplied to prisoner or counsel.

**Authority by component:**

- Qualification, representation, unitary route and transcript deferral: Source, authority and operative text, Public Law 104-132, Title I, §107(a), 28 U.S.C. §§2261, 2265, enacted 1996-04-24; the Record’s retained complete enacted text supplies these components.

**Present operation effective:** AEDPA enactment, 1996-04-24.

**Effective transition:** Under §107(c), chapter 154 applies to cases pending on or after April 24, 1996, subject to its own qualification conditions. Enactment establishes no State’s qualification, particular missed deadline, waiver, execution, stay or entitlement.

### Execution protection under qualifying chapter 154 proceedings

**Governing question:** Mandatory stays, expiration and subsequent protection under §2262.

**Current rule:** When chapter 154 applies and an appropriate state court enters a §2261(c) representation order, an execution warrant/order must be stayed upon application to a court with jurisdiction over a §2254 proceeding. The application must recite the State’s invocation of chapter 154 and the scheduled execution’s subjection to stay. The stay expires if the prisoner fails to file within §2263’s period; knowingly waives §2254 review before a competent court, after consequence advice and with counsel unless competently and knowingly waived; or timely files but fails to make a substantial showing of denial of a federal right or is denied relief in district court or later review. After one of those events, no federal court may grant another stay unless the court of appeals approves a second/successive application under §2244(b).

**Authority by component:**

- Order/application trigger, separate expiration events and successive-authorization condition: Source, authority and operative text, Public Law 104-132, Title I, §107(a), 28 U.S.C. §2262, enacted 1996-04-24; the Record’s retained complete enacted text supplies these components.

**Present operation effective:** AEDPA enactment, 1996-04-24.

**Effective transition:** Under §107(c), chapter 154 applies to cases pending on or after April 24, 1996, subject to its own qualification conditions. Enactment establishes no State’s qualification, particular missed deadline, waiver, execution, stay or entitlement.

**Related current rules:** “Qualifying State counsel systems for special capital habeas procedures” supplies the prerequisite and unitary-order substitution. General stay rules do not establish those qualifications or override an actually applicable statutory restriction.

### Capital habeas filing and claim scope under chapter 154

**Governing question:** Filing time, tolling and permissible claims when the special State system qualifies.

**Current rule:** A chapter 154 §2254 application must be filed in the appropriate district court within 180 days after final state direct-review affirmance of conviction and sentence or expiration of time to seek that review. The period is tolled from filing to disposition of a Supreme Court certiorari petition seeking review of the final state direct-review capital judgment, from filing the first state postconviction/collateral petition to its final state disposition, and for an additional period no longer than thirty days upon motion in the prospective federal district court and good cause for failing to file within the period. Under §2264, the district court considers only claims raised and decided on the merits in state court unless proper presentation failed because of unconstitutional or unlawful State action, a newly recognized Supreme Court federal right made retroactive, or a factual predicate not discoverable by due diligence in time for state or federal collateral review. It must rule on properly presented claims subject to §2254(a), (d) and (e).

**Authority by component:**

- 180-day period, distinct tolling clauses and claim-scope exceptions: Source, authority and operative text, Public Law 104-132, Title I, §107(a), 28 U.S.C. §§2263–2264, enacted 1996-04-24; the Record’s retained complete enacted text supplies these components.

**Present operation effective:** AEDPA enactment, 1996-04-24.

**Effective transition:** Under §107(c), chapter 154 applies to cases pending on or after April 24, 1996, subject to its own qualification conditions. Enactment establishes no State’s qualification, particular missed deadline, waiver, execution, stay or entitlement.

**Related current rules:** “Qualifying State counsel systems for special capital habeas procedures” supplies unitary-review substitutions and transcript-based deferral. Chapter 153’s one-year period and exceptions are not substituted for these distinct provisions.

### Adjudication periods and enforcement under chapter 154

**Governing question:** Priority, deadlines, amendment and enforcement for covered capital habeas litigation.

**Current rule:** Covered §2254 applications and §2255 motions by persons under death sentence receive priority over noncapital matters in district and appellate courts. A chapter 154 district application requires final determination and judgment within 180 days after filing, with at least 120 days for all party actions, including pleadings, briefs and any necessary hearing, before submission. One additional delay of at most thirty days is permitted by a written ends-of-justice finding outweighing the public’s and applicant’s speedy-disposition interests. The court must consider possible miscarriage of justice; unusualness/complexity making timely adequate briefing unreasonable because of defendant numbers, prosecution nature or novel issues; and otherwise unreasonable deprivation of time to obtain counsel, continuity or effective preparation with due diligence. General calendar congestion cannot justify delay. Initial, successive and remand redeterminations are covered, with the remand period running from the remand order. After an answer, amendment is allowed only on §2244(b) grounds. The deadlines create no otherwise unavailable stay and noncompliance no conviction/sentence relief. The State may seek appellate mandamus to enforce district limits; the appellate court must act within thirty days. A chapter 154 appeal must be finally determined within 120 days after the reply brief or, absent reply, answering brief. Rehearing/en-banc requests must be granted or denied within thirty days after the request or required response; if granted, final determination follows within 120 days of the grant. These appellate periods cover initial/successive applications and remand redeterminations, with remand periods starting at the remand order. They likewise create no additional stay or substantive relief; State enforcement lies by Supreme Court mandamus. District extension orders must be transmitted to the Administrative Office, whose annual congressional reports address district and appellate compliance and include those orders.

**Authority by component:**

- Priority, minimum preparation interval, deadlines, extension factors, amendment bar and enforcement: Source, authority and operative text, Public Law 104-132, Title I, §107(a), 28 U.S.C. §2266, enacted 1996-04-24; the Record’s retained complete enacted text supplies these components.

**Present operation effective:** AEDPA enactment, 1996-04-24.

**Effective transition:** Under §107(c), chapter 154 applies to cases pending on or after April 24, 1996, subject to its own qualification conditions. Enactment establishes no State’s qualification, particular missed deadline, waiver, execution, stay or entitlement.

**Exceptions and limits:** Adjudication periods do not establish qualification, a required hearing, a deadline violation or automatic substantive relief in any case. The §2255 capital-priority direction retains its express scope; it does not place every §2255 motion under the chapter’s state-case deadlines.

## Civil rights and constitutional remedies

### Individual-capacity liability for official conduct under §1983

**Governing question:** Whether use of official authority prevents a state officer from being a §1983 person when sued individually.

**Current rule:** A state officer sued in an individual capacity is a person under §1983 even when the challenged act was undertaken through official authority; sovereign immunity does not independently bar a judgment payable by the officer personally. The plaintiff must prove the officer's own federal violation under color of law, and applicable personal immunities remain available. The capacity in which the officer is sued, rather than whether the conduct was official, distinguishes this action from a claim against the State or an official-capacity damages claim.

**Authority by component:**

- Personhood, capacity distinction, personal-payment immunity limit, and retained defenses: Hafer v. Melo — Individual-capacity §1983 coverage of official conduct, November 5, 1991; O'Connor's unanimous participating opinion.

**Present operation effective:** *Hafer*, November 5, 1991.

**Holdings navigation:** Hafer v. Melo, 502 U.S. 21 (1991) — Individual-capacity liability.

### Municipal responsibility and the underlying federal deprivation

**Governing question:** Whether a municipal employee must prove an additional freestanding abuse of governmental power to recover under §1983.

**Current rule:** A municipal employee who proves deprivation of a federal right under color of state law and the required municipal responsibility need not prove an additional, independent abuse-of-governmental-power element. The federal deprivation and its attribution to municipal policy or custom remain separate required inquiries. Employment alone establishes neither municipal liability nor a substantive right; *Canton*'s training analysis supplies attribution and causation, not the underlying constitutional guarantee.

**Authority by component:**

- Rejection of the additional element and separation of deprivation from attribution: Collins v. City of Harker Heights — No extra governmental-abuse element under §1983, February 26, 1992; Part A of Stevens's opinion, joined by all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** *Collins*, February 26, 1992.

**Holdings navigation:** Collins v. City of Harker Heights, 503 U.S. 115 (1992) — Municipal liability and public employment.

### Voluntary public employment and substantive workplace safety duties

**Governing question:** Whether a voluntary public-employment relationship creates a general substantive-due-process duty to provide workplace safety.

**Current rule:** Voluntary municipal employment does not itself create the custody or deprivation of liberty that supports affirmative constitutional duties of care, and substantive due process imposes no independent general obligation to provide such employees a workplace free from unreasonable risks. A state-law safety duty, even assuming it creates a protected liberty interest, does not convert its breach alone into a substantive constitutional wrong. The underlying federal right and constitutional arbitrariness remain distinct from state-law entitlement and municipal attribution.

**Authority by component:**

- No employment-based general safety duty or custody: Collins v. City of Harker Heights — Voluntary public employment creates no general constitutional safety duty, February 26, 1992; Part B of Stevens's unanimous opinion.
- State entitlement does not alone establish arbitrary deprivation: Collins — These pleaded omissions do not establish constitutional arbitrariness, February 26, 1992; Part C joined by White, Blackmun, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, and Thomas with Stevens. Stone's distinct concurrence is not part of this component's authority.

**Present operation effective:** *Collins*, February 26, 1992.

**Open question:** Actual compulsion, deliberately inflicted bodily injury, procedural due process, and a properly alleged affirmative-danger claim are not resolved. *Collins* creates neither a general affirmative-danger test nor a categorical rejection of one.

**Holdings navigation:** Collins v. City of Harker Heights, 503 U.S. 115 (1992) — Municipal liability and public employment.

### Compensatory remedies for intentional Title IX discrimination

**Governing question:** Whether remedial silence or Spending Clause notice bars compensatory damages in the established Title IX private action.

**Current rule:** When a cognizable federal statutory cause of action exists, courts may award appropriate relief absent clear congressional direction limiting it; recognizing relief does not itself create a new cause of action. Title IX's established private action permits compensatory damages for proved intentional discrimination, subject to proof of recipient responsibility, causation, and compensable loss. The Spending Clause notice principle does not categorically bar that compensation for intentional breach of Title IX's express nondiscrimination condition.

**Authority by component:**

- Appropriate relief in an existing action and availability of Title IX compensation: Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools — Compensatory relief in the established Title IX action, February 26, 1992.
- Rejection of the categorical funding-notice bar: Franklin — Notice does not bar damages for the pleaded intentional violation, February 26, 1992. Both holdings rest on White's opinion joined by Stone, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, and Souter; Scalia and Thomas supply judgment votes only on a narrower statutory ground.

**Present operation effective:** *Franklin*, February 26, 1992.

**Open question:** The decision supplies no final recipient-attribution rule, punitive remedy, liability for unintended discriminatory effects, or resolution of genuinely ambiguous funding conditions.

**Holdings navigation:** Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools, 503 U.S. 60 (1992) — Statutory discrimination remedies.

### Private enforcement of Adoption Assistance Act reasonable-efforts and reporting clauses

**Governing question:** Private enforcement of 42 U.S.C. §671(a)(15)'s reasonable-efforts clause and §671(a)(9)'s reporting clause through §1983 or an action implied directly under the Act.

**Current rule:** Read within the Act's plan and administrative-enforcement structure, §671(a)(15) creates no individual right enforceable under §1983 to compel the asserted reasonable efforts to prevent removal or reunify families. An approved plan's commitment, §671(a)(3)'s statewide-operation requirement and caseworker deficiencies do not supply that missing right. Nor does §671(a)(15) imply a separate private action: beneficial purpose does not establish congressional intent to create the requested remedy. Section 671(a)(9) requires a plan to provide reporting to the appropriate court or law-enforcement agency when a state agency has reason to believe a child's home or institution is unsuitable because of neglect, abuse or exploitation and the child's care is paid for in whole or in part under Title IV-E or IV-B. That administrative direction does not create the asserted private §1983 right or an implied action to obtain caseworker relief. The §1983-right and implied-action inquiries remain distinct; failure to imply an action does not bar an otherwise available enacted §1983 remedy.

**Authority by component:**
- No individual §671(a)(15) right: Suter v. Artist M., March 25, 1992, “Section 671(a)(15) supplies no individual reasonable-efforts right enforceable under §1983,” Part II.
- No separate implied (15) action: the same record, “Section 671(a)(15) supplies no separate implied action,” Part III.
- Reporting trigger and absence of asserted §1983 right: the same record, “The asserted §671(a)(9) reporting claim is not enforceable through §1983,” Part IV-A.
- No implied reporting action: the same record, “The asserted §671(a)(9) claim supplies no separate implied action,” Part IV-B. White for O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas supplies six controlling joins for each component.

**Present operation effective:** Suter, March 25, 1992.

**Exceptions and limits:** No general rule makes state-plan provisions unenforceable. Administrative funding review does not necessarily foreclose an otherwise existing §1983 right, and the State's administrative obligations remain. Appropriate relief presupposes a cognizable action and cannot create the missing right or action.

**Open question:** Private enforceability of §671(a)(16), read with §675(1) and §675(5)(B), remains undecided, as do the preserved claim's merits and proper relief.

**Holdings navigation:** Suter v. Artist M., 503 U.S. 347 (1992) — Child-welfare statutory enforcement.

### Private use of state seizure procedures and qualified immunity

**Governing question:** Whether private litigants using state replevin, garnishment or attachment procedures receive public-official immunity under Harlow.

**Current rule:** Private litigants invoking those procedures do not receive Harlow's objective immunity from suit merely because qualifying joint action is attributable to the State under §1983. State attribution and immunity eligibility remain separate; reasonable reliance on legislation does not itself establish this immunity. Each defendant's attribution and other liability predicates still require independent determination.

**Authority by component:**
- Private-immunity exclusion and separate attribution: Wyatt v. Cole, “Private litigants and immunity from suit”, May 18, 1992; O'Connor, joined in full by White, Blackmun, Stevens, Scalia and Kennedy (six); Stone adds a join only for replevin and the reservations (seven at that scope).

**Present operation effective:** Wyatt v. Cole, May 18, 1992.

**Open question:** The existence and scope of a distinct good-faith or probable-cause defense, any additional plaintiff's elements and allocation of any such burden remain undecided. Eligible public officials' immunity is unchanged.

**Holdings navigation:** Wyatt v. Cole, 504 U.S. 158 (1992) — Section 1983 immunity.

### Municipal civil-rights pleading under the Federal Rules

**Governing question:** What instructions govern municipal civil-rights pleading under the Federal Rules?

**Current rule:** Courts may not impose a judge-created heightened factual-particularity requirement on municipal §1983 complaints beyond the then-operative Federal Rules. Rule 8 governs; Rule 9(b)'s fraud-or-mistake categories do not add municipal liability. Monell and Canton retain their substantive attribution and causation requirements. Rule 11, discovery control and Rule 56 remain distinct. No individual-officer pleading standard is decided.

**Authority by component:**

- The Federal Rules supply the pleading standard for municipal § 1983 claims: Leatherman v. Tarrant County Narcotics Intelligence and Coordination Unit — The Federal Rules supply the pleading standard for municipal § 1983 claims, 1993-03-03. Stone's Opinion of the Court, joined in full by White, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas; unanimous controlling authority.

**Present operation effective:** 1993-03-03; Leatherman v. Tarrant County Narcotics Intelligence and Coordination Unit, for the components identified above.

**Holdings navigation:** Leatherman v. Tarrant County Narcotics Intelligence and Coordination Unit, 507 U.S. 163 (1993).

### Private-conspiracy deprivation claims under §1985(3)

**Governing question:** What instructions govern private-conspiracy deprivation claims under §1985(3)?

**Current rule:** A purely private conspiracy under §1985(3)'s deprivation clause must aim to interfere with a right protected against private as well as official encroachment; incidental effects do not suffice. Interstate-travel interference must be a conscious objective, not simply an effect on persons who traveled. Constitutional abortion liberty does not itself protect against purely private obstruction without necessary state involvement or another privately protected right. The full nonracial-class boundary, whether women qualify and whether abortion opposition proves or excludes sex-based animus remain unresolved. The separate hindrance clause is not construed, and no categorical intrastate-obstruction rule is adopted.

**Authority by component:**

- Private conspiracy requires purposeful interference with a privately protected right: Bray v. Alexandria Women’s Health Clinic — Private conspiracy requires purposeful interference with a privately protected right, 1993-01-13. Scalia Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, White, Kennedy and Thomas: five direct supporters. Souter separately agrees with rejection of this theory without a formal join.
- Constitutional abortion liberty does not itself supply the private-right element: Bray v. Alexandria Women’s Health Clinic — Constitutional abortion liberty does not itself supply the private-right element, 1993-01-13. Scalia Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, White, Kennedy and Thomas: five direct supporters of this distinct sufficient ground addressing the alternative privacy theory. Souter separately accepts Scott’s private-right limitation.

**Present operation effective:** 1993-01-13; Bray v. Alexandria Women’s Health Clinic, for the components identified above.

**Holdings navigation:** Bray v. Alexandria Women’s Health Clinic, 506 U.S. 263 (1993); Bray v. Alexandria Women’s Health Clinic, 506 U.S. 263 (1993).

### Ministerial court reporting and absolute judicial immunity

**Governing question:** What instructions govern ministerial court reporting and absolute judicial immunity?

**Current rule:** Accurate recording and production of a verbatim transcript are ministerial functions and do not carry absolute judicial immunity merely because they are important or integral to adjudication. The claimant of immunity must establish its historical and functional justification; discretionary adjudication supplies a different function. Denial of absolute immunity establishes neither a cause of action nor liability, and other defenses remain open.

**Authority by component:**

- The ministerial transcript function does not carry absolute judicial immunity: Antoine v. Byers & Anderson, Inc. — The ministerial transcript function does not carry absolute judicial immunity, 1993-06-07. Stevens’s Opinion of the Court; Stone-Zsela, White, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas (9 Justices). Direct majority support at this level of generality; no Marks synthesis.

**Present operation effective:** 1993-06-07; Antoine v. Byers & Anderson, Inc., for the components identified above.

**Holdings navigation:** Antoine v. Byers & Anderson, Inc., 508 U.S. 429 (1993).

### Prosecutorial investigation, advocacy and press statements

**Governing question:** What instructions govern prosecutorial investigation, advocacy and press statements?

**Current rule:** Ordinary investigative work to identify a perpetrator before probable cause has no absolute prosecutorial immunity for alleged fabrication; later courtroom use does not retrospectively transform it into advocacy. Genuine evaluation and preparation in an advocate's role remain protected; neither all pre-indictment nor all post-indictment acts share one classification. Statements to the press announcing an indictment also lack absolute prosecutorial immunity merely because they concern prosecution or cause injury through subsequent proceedings. Qualified immunity, an actionable constitutional deprivation and other liability predicates remain separate.

**Authority by component:**

- Investigative fabrication is not protected by absolute prosecutorial immunity: Buckley v. Fitzsimmons — Investigative fabrication is not protected by absolute prosecutorial immunity, 1993-06-24. Stevens’s Opinion of the Court, this proposition; Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Thomas (6 Justices). Direct majority support at the stated level of generality; no Marks aggregation.
- A press conference does not carry an advocate’s absolute immunity: Buckley v. Fitzsimmons — A press conference does not carry an advocate’s absolute immunity, 1993-06-24. Stevens’s Opinion of the Court, this proposition; Stone-Zsela, White, Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas (9 Justices). **Present operation effective:** 1993-06-24; Buckley v. Fitzsimmons, for the components identified above.

**Holdings navigation:** Buckley v. Fitzsimmons, 509 U.S. 259 (1993).

### Prospective parole-consideration claims under §1983

**Governing question:** Whether a prisoner must use habeas to restore the required frequency of discretionary parole consideration.

**Current rule:** A state prisoner may seek prospective declaratory and injunctive relief under §1983 against responsible officials to restore the legally required frequency of discretionary parole consideration when the judgment neither orders release nor establishes entitlement to release or shorter custody. Habeas is not the exclusive channel for that opportunity-only claim, and no general state-remedy exhaustion requirement attaches to the properly brought §1983 action.

**Authority by component:**

- Opportunity-only channel and absence of general exhaustion: Cavanaugh v. Roller — Section 1983 permits this opportunity-only claim, 1993-11-30. Part II of O'Connor's opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, and Souter; six Justices adopt the same rule and affirm this remedial channel.

**Present operation effective:** Cavanaugh v. Roller, 1993-11-30.

**Related current rules:** “Conviction-negating damages claims and favorable invalidation” governs the separate in-custody damages prerequisite; Cavanaugh’s opportunity-only relief remains available.

**Holdings navigation:** Section 1983 permits this opportunity-only claim.

### Relevant precedent in appellate qualified-immunity review

**Governing question:** What legal sources an appellate court must consider on a preserved clearly-established-law issue.

**Current rule:** Whether a federal right was clearly established when officials acted is reviewed independently using all relevant precedent, including cases neither cited to nor discovered by the district court. This does not admit a new claim or factual record, make each considered precedent controlling or permit later decisions to supply notice retrospectively. The notice inquiry stays fixed to the conduct date. Ordinary claim and evidence preservation, particularized objective immunity and proper summary-judgment treatment remain distinct; no mandatory merits-first sequence follows.

**Authority by component:**

- Independent legal review, contemporaneous notice and preservation limits: Elder v. Holloway — Appellate review must consider all relevant law on the preserved immunity issue, 1994-02-23. Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas. All nine adopt the legal-authority rule and the limited reversal and remand.

**Present operation effective:** Elder v. Holloway, 1994-02-23.

**Holdings navigation:** Appellate review must consider all relevant law on the preserved immunity issue.

### No direct federal-agency Bivens damages action

**Governing question:** Whether sovereign consent itself permits constitutional damages against a federal agency.

**Current rule:** A waiver removes sovereign immunity but does not create constitutional damages liability. Bivens’s individual-officer action does not extend directly to a federal agency: that extension would create a new defendant and public obligation. Independently, even assuming compensation and deterrence benefits, the expansion of direct federal fiscal liability and redesign of the remedial structure counsel against judicial creation of that agency action. Existing individual Bivens, Davis and Carlson actions and genuinely authorized statutory remedies retain their own scope; no adequate substitute remedy is presumed.

**Authority by component:**

- Separation of waiver from agency cause: FDIC v. Meyer — Waiver does not create a direct agency Bivens action, 1994-02-23. The cause-of-action portion of Thomas's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg. All nine adopt this independently sufficient ground for rejecting the agency award.
- Independent fiscal-and-remedial reason against extension: FDIC v. Meyer — Independent reason to leave this fiscal and remedial extension to Congress, 1994-02-23. The independent fiscal-and-remedial portion of Thomas's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg. Nine Justices adopt this independently sufficient alternative ground.

**Present operation effective:** FDIC v. Meyer, 1994-02-23.

**Holdings navigation:** Waiver does not create a direct agency Bivens action.

### The 1991 Civil Rights Act’s new liabilities and jury election

**Governing question:** Whether the 1991 Act’s new damages and contractual coverage reach preenactment conduct.

**Current rule:** Section 102’s new compensatory and punitive damages do not apply to conduct before November 21, 1991. Its jury election exists only when statutory damages under that section are available and requested; either party may then demand a jury, which must not be told the statutory caps. Section 102 damages supplement rather than duplicate §706(g) relief and exclude backpay, interest on backpay and other relief authorized there. Punitive damages require malice or reckless indifference to federally protected rights and are unavailable against governments, government agencies and political subdivisions. Section 101’s expansion of §1981 to contractual performance, modification, termination and enjoyment of benefits likewise does not govern preenactment conduct. Corrective purpose alone supplies no contrary temporal command; a defendant need not prove actual reliance on the former interpretation.

**Authority by component:**

- New damages, their limits and dependent jury election: Landgraf v. USI Film Products — Section 102 does not add its new damages to this preenactment conduct; The jury election depends on an available statutory damages claim, 1994-04-26. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas independently reach the same unavailability of new damages through their concurrence. Blackmun disagrees about compensation and reserves punitive damages. Stevens’s jury portion, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Souter and Ginsburg, supplies the controlling five-Justice explanation. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas reach the same conditional conclusion in their concurrence; Blackmun would permit a jury election because he would make compensation available.

Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas accept the judicial/legislative distinction through their separate textual method, not through a presumed full join.
